articles.title: Trump picks Stephen Miller as chief of staff, signaling intent to stay the course
articles.summary: By Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose, Steve Holland and Trevor Hunnicutt WASHINGTON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump named longtime aide Stephen Miller as his chief of staff on Friday, giving the architect of some of his toughest domestic policies one of the most powerful jobs in Washington after Republicans lost control of Congress. Miller, who will replace Susie Wiles, assumes the role as the president prepares to confront ‌a Democratic-led House of Representatives and Senate and a wave of congressional investigations into his administration. A longtime proponent of expansive presidential authority, Miller takes over at a moment when the Republican Party's defeat in Tuesday's ‌midterm elections could leave Trump more reliant on executive power to advance his domestic agenda. In a social media post, Trump called Miller "one of my most trusted advisors," and praised Wiles for doing "an outstanding job." Trump said the change would take effect on Monday. A White House official said Miller's appointment signals ​that Trump has no intention of rethinking his policies and instead is rewarding his most loyal aides. "He's not changing course," the official said, despite tens of millions of American voters repudiating Trump's domestic agenda and foreign policy. Trump said this week he was willing to work with Democrats on Capitol Hill. But elevating Miller, who is known for being caustic and uncompromising, could signal a more confrontational approach and a renewed push to advance the president's agenda on immigration and other issues, several White House officials said. Trump had been displeased with his political and communications operations in the run-up to Tuesday's election as his public approval ratings fell near record lows. This week, he said the White House needed to be "more aggressive" as Democrats retake congressional power, ‌according to a person briefed on the matter. "The mission now is more clear than ⁠ever," Miller said on X after his appointment. "Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic." Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to become the new Democratic speaker of the House, responded to the announcement by calling Miller a "reckless extremist" in a posting on X. MILLER DRIVING IMMIGRATION CRACKDOWN Miller, 41, is one of Trump's longest-serving aides and one of ⁠only a few who served throughout his first and second terms in office. Since Trump's return to the White House in 2025, Miller has officially served as deputy chief of staff under Wiles, but he has wielded outsize influence across much of Trump's domestic agenda and has had the president's ear. He is perhaps best known for driving Trump's aggressive immigration crackdown, setting a goal of 3,000 arrests a day. The efforts to meet that target pushed masked US immigration officers into communities around the country, increasingly arresting people with no criminal ​records ​and who had been living in the country for decades. The crackdown, however, gets poor marks with Americans. Just 36% of respondents to ​a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed early this week approve of it, with 54% disapproving. Representative Robert Garcia, ‌the top Democrat on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, said the party planned to investigate Miller's immigration policies. "Stephen Miller should lawyer up," he said. Miller was also deeply involved in Trump's campaign to remake the federal bureaucracy, which led to the dismissal of tens of thousands of civil servants in 2025. He was also a driving force behind the administration's battles with universities, diversity programs and other institutions. HAWKISH FOREIGN POLICY On foreign policy, Miller has been a vocal supporter of Trump's deadly military strikes on boats suspected of carrying drugs in the Caribbean and Pacific, a campaign that has raised legal questions. He has also praised US and Israeli strikes in Iran and defended a naval blockade and sanctions as ways to weaken Tehran and curb its ability to threaten its neighbors. It is not clear whether that is still his view after voters punished Republicans this week in part for the economic fallout from the Iran war. Marc Short, who was chief ‌of staff to then-Vice President Mike Pence in Trump's first term, said that in Miller, Trump is "getting someone who is wed to him" ​and who is willing to battle Congress over issues like immigration and congressional investigations. "It would not suggest that there is high expectation for bipartisan ​legislation," Short said in an interview. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, who faces Democratic calls for impeachment over the ​Iran war, celebrated Miller's promotion with a social media post reading, "Patriots in control," reflecting the enthusiasm of some Trump allies for putting Miller in a position of greater authority. SHAKE UP AFTER ELECTION ‌SETBACK The chief of staff typically wields great influence as the president's gatekeeper. The person ​manages White House staff, organizes the president's time and schedule, and ​oversees other government departments and lawmakers. Wiles, 69, who submitted her resignation on Thursday night, will move to Trump's political operation, according to a White House official. The veteran political operative from Florida was the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff. She brought decades of political experience to the role and was regarded as running a more disciplined operation than some of Trump's prior top aides. She maintained her role even ​while undergoing treatment earlier this year for early-stage breast cancer. Wiles rarely challenged Trump's policies ‌but brought discipline to an often chaotic operation and was seen as a voice of reason. Her exit raises questions about who will play her role. Trump ran through four chiefs of staff – an unusually ​high number – during his 2017-2021 term, as they were seen to have struggled to rein in the unpredictable president. (Reporting by Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose, Steve Holland, Jacob Bogage in Washington; Additional reporting by ​Bhargav Acharya and Susan Heavey; Writing by Trevor Hunnicutt; editing by Scott Malone, Colleen Jenkins, Ross Colvin and Jonathan Spicer) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-promotes-stephen-miller-post-190429829.html

articles.title: Elizabeth Warren's new Senate role puts Wall Street and Trump on notice for hearings
articles.summary: Democratic firebrand Elizabeth Warren, a consumer advocate known for her fierce battles over financial regulations, will take the gavel in January to become chair of the powerful Senate Banking Committee. According to a source familiar with her plans, the Massachusetts senator intends to use her expanded platform to advance legislation to tackle populist affordability issues with a focus on housing. The person familiar with her plans says Warren will use the committee's investigative powers to hold hearings and launch investigations into executive branch ethics and corporate practices, aiming to hold President Trump, the administration, Wall Street, and Big Tech accountable for economic decisions she views as having driven up costs for consumers. Warren is also expected to take steps to shield the Federal Reserve from White House overreach . Any future nominee for the Fed will have to go through her committee. Earlier this year, she rallied Democrats to oppose Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's confirmation before the banking committee, stalling his eventual confirmation. Wall Street is likely to be another of Warren's targets. Before Republicans regained control of Congress, Democrats would have the chief executives of big banks testify before the Senate Banking and House Financial Services committees once a year. The banking industry can expect a return to that practice. Stephen Biggar, who covers the financial sector for Argus Research, says hearings will offer more transparency, but won't be accompanied by meaningful rulemaking. Biggar expects increased oversight, potentially more consumer protections, and actions to limit banks' market share size, such as blocking mergers. He added that there are concerns that the deregulation efforts and lower capital requirements for banks championed by Republicans are now at risk. James Angel, an associate professor at Georgetown University's McDonough School of Business, said he thinks the hearings will accomplish two things: producing information and sound bites that will get people to pay attention and galvanize public opinion. Second, Angel says they will serve as a deterrent for people in power. "If people will be held under oath and there's a prospect of perjury, that will deter people from doing 'Trumpier' things," Angel said in an interview. Angel also noted that any Trump appointee who has to be confirmed by Warren's committee will need to withstand bipartisan scrutiny and thus is more likely to be a moderate. Prediction markets, housing, AI, and credit card rates This summer, Warren teamed up with current Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott to pass a sprawling bipartisan housing bill that addresses housing affordability by encouraging more homebuilding, expanding financing options, and restricting large corporate investors buying single-family homes. Warren is expected to continue her push to rein in private equity across industries that she sees jacking up costs for families. Warren also intends to conduct oversight into prediction markets and election betting platforms to prevent insider trading and platform manipulation. Before the midterm elections, Warren co-authored a letter with Utah Sen. John Curtis to executives of Kalshi and Polymarket asking them to explain how they would prevent candidates, campaign staff, and others with inside information from trading on election contracts. There are also potential areas of common ground with Republicans, including advancing bipartisan AI export-control bills. Warren worked on three such bills this year, including a measure to stop advanced AI chips from being used by China to develop dangerous systems. One area of agreement that could secure Trump's signature: capping credit card interest rates. It's something both Warren and Trump support, along with newly elected Democrats, including Texas's new senator, James Talarico. Follow Jennifer Schonberger on X @Jenniferisms and on Instagram . articles.title: 2 DOJ officials resign, including attorney who oversaw 'grand conspiracy' probe
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — The top federal prosecutor in Miami who had been tasked with overseeing an investigation into foes of President Donald Trump has resigned, joining other high-profile Justice Department officials departing in the wake of the midterm elections, officials said Friday. Jason Reding Quiñones' resignation follows frustrations among Washington officials with his management of the office assigned to lead the so-called "grand conspiracy" investigation, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel issues. The Justice Department's top national security official, John Eisenberg, also resigned on Friday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said. On Thursday, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led a radical overhaul of the department's Civil Rights Division , also announced her departure. Quiñones was confirmed by the Senate last year as U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, where the Justice Department had centered its meandering probe into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired against the Republican president. His departure comes as the investigation has shown signs of faltering amid a spate of staff turnovers and delays. Investigators in recent weeks have put off scheduled grand jury testimony of several witnesses, according to multiple people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation. Blanche said in a social media post that the department is grateful for Quiñones' "leadership in combating violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking, and transnational crime, including the indictment of Raúl Castro." Castro, the former Cuban president, was indicted by Quiñones' office in May on charges related to the 1996 downing of civilian planes flown by Miami-based exiles. Quiñones said Friday that he is leaving with "immense pride in what we accomplished together and profound gratitude for the opportunity to serve our great Nation." "I am grateful to President Trump for his trust and to the extraordinary men and women of the great Southern District of Florida for their dedication, friendship, and unwavering commitment to justice and the rule of law," Quiñones wrote in a social media post. The "grand conspiracy" investigation has proceeded in fits and starts for over a year with repeated setbacks and departures. Last April, a lead national security prosecutor in the investigation of former CIA Director John Brennan was replaced on the team after raising questions about the strength of the case. Shortly afterward, Joseph diGenova, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, took over the probe. DiGenova resigned from the Justice Department in September without bringing any criminal charges. Eisenberg was sworn in as assistant attorney general in charge of the department's National Security Division in June 2025 and oversaw cases involving espionage, terrorism, export control violations, cyber crimes and other matters. Among the division's most high-profile cases under his watch was the prosecution of former national security adviser John Bolton, who pleaded guilty this year to allegations of mishandling classified information and is awaiting sentencing. "He has served with distinction, strengthening our nation's ability to address threats, both foreign and domestic," Blanche said in a statement. articles.title: Democrats take full control of Arizona government for 1st time in 60 years
articles.summary: PHOENIX (AP) — Democrats in Arizona won control of both legislative chambers and retained the governor's office, giving the party its first trifecta in the state since 1966 as Democrats made major gains nationwide in this week's elections and took control of both chambers of Congress . In her first term, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs had vetoed more than 540 measures passed by the Republican-led Legislature on policies including taxes, immigration and voting laws. Hobbs has said she's looking to address water issues and affordability, and take on fraud and abuse in the state's school voucher program. The Associated Press called enough legislative races to confirm that both chambers flipped on Friday. The news organization calls races individually and it can take several days after voting, depending on when election officials tally the votes and how close the elections are. There have not been major disputes or disruptions this year. In Arizona, Republicans have held the House for 60 years and the Senate since the early 1990s. Overall, Democrats took full control — both statehouse chambers and governors' offices — in at least six states where they previously shared power with Republicans. Besides Arizona, those wins were in the battleground states of Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Wisconsin. The flips weren't just in states that are normally competitive. Democrats won control of the Texas House, which Republicans have held since 2003, and elected Gina Hinojosa as the state's first Democratic governor since George W. Bush ousted Ann Richards in 1994. Republicans held onto the state Senate. Democrats also flipped the lower chambers of the legislatures in Maine and North Carolina and both chambers in New Hampshire, where Republican Kelly Ayotte was reelected. The count could grow as results are tallied in additional states. The National Council of State Legislatures says it's likely to end up as the election with the most legislative seats and chambers changing parties since the 2010 election, when Republicans took over governments across the country amid the Great Recession. Democrats will also hold the governor's office in at least 28 states. Results are still pending in Alaska and Kansas. articles.title: New DNA technology could solve JonBenét Ramsey's killing 30 years later
articles.summary: In the early hours of Dec. 26, 1996, after a festive family Christmas, Patsy Ramsey walked down the stairs in her Boulder, Colorado, home to discover a terrifying ransom note telling her that her 6-year-old daughter JonBenét Ramsey had been kidnapped. She immediately called 911 and the Boulder Police Department responded to the scene in three minutes. Courtesy of John Andrew Ramsey - PHOTO: JonBenét Ramsey was 6 years old when she was found dead in her home in Boulder, Co. on Dec. 26, 1996. The taunting two-and-a-half-page ransom note was addressed to JonBenét's father, John Ramsey, and demanded $118,000 for the safe return of his daughter. "You stand a 99% chance of killing your daughter if you try to out smart [sic] us," the letter said. There was no sign of JonBenét or further communication from the would-be kidnappers. A new "20/20" episode, "JonBenét Ramsey: Race Against Time, Who is 'Unknown Male 1?' -- A New Diane Sawyer Investigation" airing Friday, Nov. 6 at 9 p.m. ET on ABC and streaming the next day on Disney+ and Hulu, re-examines the case. You can get more behind the scenes of each week's episode by listening to "20/20: The After Show" weekly series right on your 20/20 podcast feed on Mondays, hosted by "20/20" co-anchor Deborah Roberts. Hours later, a police officer asked John Ramsey and a friend to look through the house to see if anything seemed out of place. John Ramsey discovered his daughter's lifeless body in the basement of their home. DNA testing confirms 'serial killer' in Pennsylvania in 1970s: State police An autopsy report determined that JonBenét had been sexually assaulted and killed by blunt force trauma to the head and strangulation, which was carried out with a makeshift corded torture device called a garrote. With 19 new interviews, ABC News anchor Diane Sawyer and chief investigative correspondent Aaron Katersky take a fresh look at this cold case, talking with investigators, forensic scientists, genealogy experts, the Boulder Police chief and JonBenét's brothers Burke Ramsey and John Andrew Ramsey, among others. Courtesy of John Andrew Ramsey - PHOTO: JonBenét Ramsey with her mother, Patsy Ramsey, both of whom competed in pageants. In the weeks and months after the murder, members of the Ramsey family came under intense scrutiny by both the Boulder police and the general public. Skeptics of the family pointed to several details of the case, including the ransom note, which some close to the investigation believed was staged by a family member to cover up JonBenét's death. The note was written on Patsy Ramsey's notepad but after numerous handwriting comparisons, only one indicated that the samples showed any similarities to Patsy's writing. The Ramsey family vehemently denied any claims they were involved in their daughter's death. In 2008, DNA was detected on the outside of JonBenét's pajama bottoms using a new testing method called touch DNA analysis. It matched the DNA found inside JonBenét's underwear and traced to the same unknown male, and not to any member of the Ramsey family. ABC News - PHOTO: ABC News anchor Diane Sawyer and chief investigative correspondent Aaron Katersky reinvestigated JonBenét Ramsey's case with new interviews. Nancy Guthrie abduction: FBI analyzing DNA recovered from her home, sources say With this development, then-Boulder County District Attorney Mary Lacy wrote a letter to John Ramsey. "This new scientific evidence convinces us that it is appropriate, given the circumstances of this case, to state that we do not consider your immediate family, including you, your wife, Patsy, and your son, Burke, to be under any suspicion in the commission of this crime," Lacy wrote. "I wish we could have done so before Mrs. Ramsey died." Patsy Ramsey died from ovarian cancer in 2006 , two years before Mary Lacy's letter to the family. Later, some Boulder officials said Lacy's letter was inappropriate for a prosecutor, and she should not have cleared the Ramseys while the investigation was ongoing. In recent years, a new technology called single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) has made it possible to solve cold murder cases nationwide . The advanced testing can retrieve DNA from miniscule samples. Combined with genetic genealogy, it allows officials to identify suspects by matching DNA to that of distant family members in law enforcement databases, using online genetic databases. Courtesy of John Andrew Ramsey - PHOTO: The Ramsey family has searched for JonBenét Ramsey's murderer for 30 years. How a man murdered his estranged wife and fled state with teen girlfriend Even with this promising new development, challenges remain for investigators. Some DNA samples obtained from the body and crime scene are very small and complex, as multiple DNA strands are mixed together, making it difficult to verifiably match with a single individual. The current Boulder Police Chief Stephen Redfearn had never before done an interview about the Ramsey case. He sat down with ABC News' Sawyer, telling her that his department is in talks with labs that might be able to test the DNA using forensic genetic genealogy. JonBenét Ramsey's father says advances in DNA technology can help police solve daughter's 1996 murder He said they are hesitant to send any sample until they have full confidence that the technology is advanced enough to get results that help progress the case. In some cases, if the sample is very small, it can be consumed by the testing. "We might get lucky because we may only, in some circumstances, with what we have, have one shot at getting it tested," Redfearn said. Redfearn said they are re-interviewing suspects, testing new evidence and pursuing every lead. "I would love nothing more than 30 years since this little girl was murdered in her own home, someone finally decides to get something off their chest," he said. JonBenét Ramsey case gets renewed attention ABC News - PHOTO: Burke Ramsey, JonBenét's brother, gave an exclusive interview after largely staying out of the public eye since his sister's murder. Burke Ramsey, who has largely stayed out of the public eye since his sister's death, praised his parents for how strong they were in the aftermath of the tragedy. "This awful thing happened to this family, and the world turns against you. And it's cruel," he said. ABC News - PHOTO: John Andrew Ramsey, JonBenét Ramsey's half brother, has sought justice for his half sister's murder for three decades. JonBenét's older half-brother, John Andrew Ramsey, said investigators must have courage and act aggressively to get the case solved as soon as possible. "I know we're going to find this person," he said. "This is a case that can be solved. There's a mountain of evidence out there. We've got the DNA testing that's in our favor. It's not a question of if, but when." This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/dna-tech-could-solve-jonben-182509064.html

articles.title: Polar vortex could bring an early blast of winter to the eastern U.S.
articles.summary: The polar vortex is weakening unusually early, forecasters have said, with a rare disruption possible within days that could send Arctic air traveling south over North America. The polar vortex is a band of powerful winds in the stratosphere that circle the North Pole each winter. It keeps the coldest air locked high in the atmosphere until it is disrupted. Once the vortex weakens, pockets of that air can be pushed south, which can bring frostier temperatures to parts of the U.S. In its updated November outlook, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) Climate Prediction Center said a disruption of the polar vortex could occur within days, possibly developing into a sudden stratospheric warming, which it called "very rare" for November. It warned that if this happens, its effects could last up to two months. The polar vortex made its mark this January, when a lobe of Arctic air pushed south, bringing a deep freeze to the eastern U.S. and Canada. Parts of northern Minnesota fell to -43°F on Jan. 24, according to state climate data , with states like Indiana also experiencing record lows as Greenland's west coast recorded its warmest January on record . NOAA said any effects in the eastern U.S. could compete with the influence of El Niño, which is still steering its outlook toward a milder November for much of the country. Here's what we know so far — and what that could mean for your weather. What does it mean for the weather? While strong sudden stratospheric warmings can disrupt the vortex and start the chain of events that sends the blasts of cold air down to North America, the jury is still out on whether the latest disruption will do this. This NOAA graphic shows what happens when the polar vortex weakens. NOAA At NOAA's winter outlook briefing on Oct. 15, Jon Gottschalck, a branch chief at the Climate Prediction Center, said the combination of a strong El Niño and a westerly wind pattern high in the tropical atmosphere typically favors a stronger, more stable polar vortex, and in turn, fewer Arctic air outbreaks. He added that cold outbreaks should still be expected at times, but with more warmer-than-normal days overall. If it takes hold, NOAA said the eastern U.S. is where effects could be felt, but El Niño's influence could compete against that. The climate phenomenon, which is currently in full swing and is expected to stay strong through at least late winter, warms the Pacific Ocean and generally brings milder weather to the U.S. There is a high chance it will become the strongest since records began in 1950. NOAA said that as the polar vortex approaches, it's worth getting prepared. "There is no cause to be alarmed when you hear about the polar vortex, but you should be prepared for colder temperatures," its guidance said. "Check the forecast for your area on weather.gov to ensure you are dressed appropriately. It is also a good idea to check the items in your home and car emergency kits at the beginning of each winter season to ensure you are prepared for any type of hazardous winter weather," the agency added. Why is the polar vortex weakening so early? The polar vortex normally strengthens through the fall as the Arctic cools, creating a whirlpool of air above the North Pole, which is why a breakdown in November would be so unusual. The vortex weakens in summer and strengthens in winter, with the winds forming miles above the North Pole. It holds its position in the Arctic until around December or January. It can be disrupted when big swells of air from lower in the atmosphere bump into it from below, making it wobble and slow down. The big disruptions, known as a "sudden stratospheric warming," usually occur in deep winter, and can stretch or split the vortex, displacing the cold air and sending it further south. If a major warming occurs within the coming days, it could be one of the earliest disruptions on record, experts told the Scientific American . The earliest polar vortex weakening previously recorded was Nov. 28, 1968. "As a weather fan, this is a big event because it's so unprecedented," Judah Cohen, a climatologist at Massachusetts Institute of Technology told the publication. articles.title: Meghan Markle's father Thomas arrested on charges related to child sexual abuse material
articles.summary: Meghan Markle's estranged father, Thomas Markle, was arrested in Florida on Friday on charges related to child sexual abuse material, authorities said. Markle, 82, was arrested by the FBI at a care home near Tampa, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California said in a press release . He was charged with one count of possession of child pornography. Authorities said Markle was arrested after agents discovered approximately 78 items — including slides, film negatives, and books — that contained suspected child sexual abuse material (CSAM) while searching two storage units registered to Markle, at least one of which was in the Los Angeles area. "Mr. Markle is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls," First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli said. "These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law." The statement said that, in October 2026, law enforcement learned that an individual signed an affidavit regarding the discovery of suspected CSAM among Markle's possessions in the Philippines. Officers then interviewed a separate individual who revealed Markle had rented a storage unit in the Los Angeles area. This led to the discovery of a second storage unit. Both had been rented by Markle since 2008. FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that “Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions.” “This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide,” Patel added. If convicted, Markle would face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison. He is expected to appear in court in Tampa on Friday. "This case highlights the importance of the involvement of the public, even if it's a family member or close friend, to be vigilant and speak up if they have information on individuals they suspect may be preying on and exploiting our children," said Patrick Grandy, the assistant director in charge of the FBI's Los Angeles Field Office. In October, it was reported that Markle was under investigation in the Philippines over allegations that he possessed child sexual abuse material. He has not been charged by police in the Philippines. The Sun first reported that his son, Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jr., told Philippine police that after his father left the country in May, he discovered images of child sexual abuse material among boxes at his father's former home in Cebu. Markle Sr. denied those allegations, telling the Daily Mail on Oct. 23: "It's just a bunch of lies. It's sick." Markle is believed to have returned to the U.S. in May, after his left leg was amputated in the Philippines in December 2025.  In October, The Sun reported Markle moved into Maravida Senior Living care home, a facility which specializes in "memory care." Meghan Markle released a statement following the claims, saying she was "deeply distressed." She also revealed that in 2019 she received a copy of a letter containing "troubling" allegations about him, which had been sent to London's Metropolitan Police. "It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," she said. British police subsequently said it had not shared the letter with other law enforcement agencies. According to the Sun on Sunday , Meghan was advised that speaking publicly could jeopardize any potential legal case. Addressing her decision to keep Archie and Lilibet away from their grandfather over the past few years, Meghan said that "any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them." She added: "My sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children." Meghan reportedly wrote to her estranged father in December 2025 to tell him she was aware of child abuse allegations against him and would not allow him to meet his grandchildren. Meghan reportedly told her father the letter would be the last time he heard from her. articles.title: GOP's losses will raise pressure on conservative Supreme Court justices to retire
articles.summary: The GOP’s sweeping losses in the midterm elections Tuesday set up an unsettling possibility for the party: If it doesn’t act now to confirm a new Supreme Court justice, it may not have another chance for years to come. That prospect is likely to ramp up pressure on the court’s two oldest conservatives - Justices Samuel A. Alito Jr., 76, and Clarence Thomas, 78 - to retire during the lame-duck period, while Republicans still have the votes to get a nominee confirmed by the Senate. The new Senate, in which Democrats will hold a majority, is seated on Jan. 3. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Alito, who joined the court in 2006, said last month he has no plans to retire during the lame-duck session. Thomas has said in the past he has no plans to step down from the court. He joined the court in 1991 and could become the longest-serving justice in its history in 2028. But given the magnitude of Democratic inroads in the Senate, legal and political experts said it could be 2033 before Republicans have a realistic shot at winning back enough seats in that chamber to approve a conservative justice. At that point, Alito and Thomas would be well into their 80s. Neither responded to a request for comment. “I think both have been making an implicit bet that they will live long enough … so that a Republican president can replace them with someone ideologically similar,” said Ed Whelan, a conservative attorney and senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center. This is likely to make many Republicans antsy, particularly those mindful of the lesson of Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, who died while still on the bench at 87, in September 2020. The liberal justice’s death allowed Republicans to move the court in a more conservative direction when they confirmed Justice Amy Coney Barrett to replace her weeks later. President Donald Trump nominated Barrett to replace Ginsburg, and over the vociferous objections of Democrats, Senate Republicans quickly muscled the nomination through just ahead of the 2020 presidential election. Trump remade the court with three picks in his first term - Barrett, Neil M. Gorsuch and Brett M. Kavanaugh - who pushed the court sharply to the right. The Supreme Court’s conservative 6-3 supermajority has delivered historic opinions on abortion, affirmative action, religious rights and much more that have thrilled Republicans. A younger replacement for Alito or Thomas could lock that advantage in for years to come. Liberals accused Republicans of hypocrisy for rapidly confirming Barrett after they blocked President Barack Obama’s nomination of Merrick Garland for 11 months in 2016, saying it was too close to the presidential election to confirm him. Trump won the White House, and Garland’s nomination was scuttled. Some observers think the window has already closed for Trump to nominate a fourth justice, which would allow him to leave a mark on the Supreme Court that few presidents have enjoyed. Republicans control 53 seats in the upper chamber, compared with 47 held by Democrats. But that split will shift to 52-48 as soon as Dec. 15, when Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) is seated as a result of a special election. A handful of moderate Senate Republicans like Maine’s Susan Collins and Alaska’s Lisa Murkowski might also have to be persuaded to back a Trump pick. The margin of error is thin enough that Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) posted Tuesday night on X that Trump probably won’t be able to get a suitable nominee confirmed. “Chance of confirming a worthy successor to Justice Thomas and/or Alito during President Trump’s term: Zero,” DeSantis wrote. “Chance of confirming a worthy successor during a hypothetical GOP admin 2029-2033: probably zero (GOP won’t be able to recapture enough seats in 28).” Harry Litman, a law professor at UCLA and a former U.S. attorney, said the optics of a justice retiring during the lame-duck session would also tarnish his or her reputation. “It would be the most crass and nakedly political resignation in the court’s history,” Litman said. Emily Hampsten, a spokeswoman for Sen. Dick Durbin (Illinois), the Democratic whip and a member of the Judiciary Committee, said a lame-duck nominee would create a backlash among voters and Democrats. “The American people will hold them accountable in 2028, and Democrats could justifiably refuse to confirm any Trump nominees for the next two years,” Hampsten said. That would curtail one of Trump’s other biggest legacies - the nomination of hundreds of lower court federal judges. Steve Vladeck, a Georgetown law professor, wrote on his blog that a lame-duck confirmation fight might also backfire on the GOP by building support for court reforms that Democrats are already eyeing during the next Congress. “The question would no longer be whether the Court deserves to be restructured, but whether the other side has left Democrats any choice,” Vladeck wrote. Gabe Roth, executive director of the reform group Fix the Court, said he thinks only small reforms will be possible while Trump is still president over the next two years. “Democrats would do well to focus on areas within the realm of court reform where there’s already strong bipartisan support,” Roth said. “That includes banning stock trading in the federal courts, adding more lower court judgeships to relieve ballooning caseloads, improving workplace conduct protections for judiciary staff and making access to court records free.” Speculation over whether Alito would retire flared over the summer when NPR published an erroneous account saying he was planning on stepping down. The story was later retracted. Alito said during a round of interviews to promote his new book last month that he had no plans to retire during the current term, which will end in June or July. The justice said he has more to contribute to the court but did consider whether to continue each term. “I intend to stick around through this term,” Alito said in the interview before the Supreme Court’s new term began last month. “I made that decision many months ago.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/05/gops-losses-will-raise-pressure-conservative-supreme-court-justices-retire/

articles.title: Vance faces a 2028 dilemma as Republicans question his ties to Trump
articles.summary: The fight for the 2028 Republican primary is beginning to take shape on the heels of the GOP's devastating midterm losses, with Vice President Vance facing criticism for blaming the losses on the Iran war and other big-name Republicans appearing to stake out their own positions. The losses have created a huge opening for GOP White House hopefuls, including Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas), to go against Vance. It’s a fact seemingly recognized by Vance, who was quick to blame the Iran war for the historic drubbings, and Republicans at large. “The election results were bad news for every leader across the party, given the scale of the losses, but they were particularly tough for Vance’s 2028 prospects,” said Kevin Madden, the veteran Republican strategist who served as a senior adviser on Mitt Romney's 2012 presidential campaign. “Vance is now in the position of serving as a loyal vice president to a lame-duck president whose approval rating is in the 30’s and whose influence on the future of the party could be in question,” Madden added. Vance has long been seen as the front-runner to succeed President Trump as the GOP standard-bearer. A close second has been Secretary of State Marco Rubio. But questions are now being raised by Republicans over whether a candidate not directly tied to the administration would be stronger. “Tuesday made clear that the stink on Vice President Vance and Secretary [Marco] Rubio may be too much to overcome as the election was a referendum on the job they are doing,” said one top GOP operative who has spoken to DeSantis. “This certainly creates a lane for DeSantis, Cruz and others if they are willing to run in a potentially impossible year to win,” the operative added. In blaming the losses on Iran, Vance put some daylight between himself and his boss. Trump, for his part, has doubled down in insisting his administration made the right decision to start the war. “Vance’s profile as a candidate is directly tied to the Trump legacy. A candidate for 2028 without an ability to craft a more unique, independent profile of their own will face challenges in this next two-year cycle,” Madden predicted. The GOP operative who spoke to The Hill said 2028 “is going to be a difficult year for Republican presidential contenders if there aren’t substantial changes.” If there aren’t changes, the operative said DeSantis might wait until 2032 to run for president. DeSantis over the last 48 hours or so has certainly sounded like someone with the White House on his mind. The Florida governor, who unsuccessfully challenged Trump for the Republican nomination in 2024, was among the first this week to offer his own pointed view on what went wrong for GOP candidates, pointing to the war in Iran and high gas prices. In an interview with SiriusXM host Stephen A. Smith, he accused some in his party of “gaslighting” voters by not acknowledging their economic anxiety. DeSantis has also pointed out that the red wall in Florida, where the GOP won a Senate race and a gubernatorial contest, held. That’s an argument that would seem to point toward his leadership of the state. Republicans did lose three House races in districts that were redrawn to give GOP candidates an edge, and they are behind in a fourth. The gubernatorial and Senate races were also closer than expected. But DeSantis can certainly make an argument about his state being a GOP bastion. Cruz ahead of the elections had been more transparent about his ambition to run for president, saying he would entertain the idea of a 2028 run after the midterms. On his podcast, Cruz compared the losses to the drubbing Republicans took after Watergate, a comparison that would seem to at least raise the issue of corruption as being a factor in the GOP’s terrible night. He also criticized the Trump tariffs and the Iran war for raising costs. “Food is too high. Gas is too high. Diesel is too high. Insurance is too high. Life is too high,” he said. GOP strategists predict that after Tuesday’s results, their primary will be wide open. “Vance is completely unacceptable to any Republican who can accurately assess the reasons for the pasting we received on Tuesday,” one former Trump campaign aide said. “It not only opens the door for others, it should soundly shut the door for JD Vance.” Other Republicans say Tuesday’s results force Vance to stake his claim early or face the consequences of a more crowded field. “Vance needs to announce first with the president’s endorsement,” said Susan Del Percio, the veteran Republican strategist. “If he doesn’t do it in January, it’ll look like a sign of weakness and everyone will know the president isn’t on board. And that’s the million dollar question: Is he out of favor with the president?” One former Trump aide — who asked for anonymity to offer a candid assessment — said that right now, there’s “more space than less space” for other Republicans to enter the race. “Let’s face it, Cruz and DeSantis were the winners in our party the other night,” the former aide said. “This is absolutely the beginning of the end of the Trump era." The former aide added that Trump “is still going to be a potent force in the primary. If he endorses you, that’s 30 percent right off the bat." But the former aide predicted it would be difficult for Vance to keep his distance from Trump and that he would be pigeonholed to his stances. “Imagine, he’s going to have to answer to Trump’s whim or rant of the day every day,” the former aide said. “And he’s not going to stand in stark contrast to the president because Trump will shred him. “That’s just not an enviable place,” the former aide added. Since the elections, Vance has been under scrutiny from both Republicans and Democrats. Former White House press secretary Ari Fleischer, who served under former President George W. Bush, took to social platform X to counter Vance’s evaluation of the sweeping GOP losses. “Please allow me to present a different perspective,” Fleischer said. “The problem was not the Iran War. It was the cease fire. If you start a war, you need to win it and finish it - otherwise don’t start it.” Democrats also pounced on Vance’s remarks. “For you to reduce it to a simple political calculation while we still have 50,000 troops in the Middle East, is one of the most crass, cynical things I’ve seen,” Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), wrote Wednesday on X. “You and President Trump got us into this war without a clear objective and without regard for the will of the American people. It’s cost us American lives and billions of dollars of American treasure with no end in sight.” On Thursday, as political pundits were saying it was the end of the Trump era, Republicans said Vance’s political future remained murky at best. “I think if you’re Vance you gotta take the nomination and pray you get someone on the other side like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez,” the first former Trump aide said, referring to the progressive representative from New York. For now, Del Percio said, results aside, Vance “ultimately stands in the same place he did three weeks ago.” “He only exists at the whim of the president,” she said. “And if Trump doesn’t endorse, will Vance go without the president’s endorsement? If he’s forced to do that, he will break with Trump and it will get ugly.” Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. articles.title: Data centers get blamed for soaring electric bills. A new study points elsewhere.
articles.summary: On Tuesday, Americans voted overwhelmingly against data centers and artificial intelligence growth. In 40 of 41 local ballot races around the country, many in the state of Ohio, voters opted to restrict or prohibit new data center constructions in their areas. Much of the growing opposition to data centers has come from rising electricity prices , which are squeezing Americans in a time of already high prices and cost of living. But, according to a new study by researchers at Harvard University and the University of Pennsylvania, data centers are probably having only a small effect on residential electricity prices. The researchers calculated that these operations were responsible for just 4 percent of the utility rate increases over the last five years. Get Climate Coach newsletter News and guidance on climate, science and technology. Sign up for free “Even to me it was somewhat surprising,” said Serguei Netessine, professor at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania and one of the study’s authors. In the run-up to the elections, Democrats pointed to data centers — and Republican support for their development — as key drivers of electricity price increases. In one campaign ad , Democrat James Talarico, now senator-elect of Texas, said that Texans were “paying the price with skyrocketing utility bills.” Sherrod Brown, Democratic senator-elect of Ohio, similarly argued that state residents were facing higher electricity bills due to the build-out of energy-hogging data centers. There are certainly some areas — like in Pennsylvania, Virginia, Ohio and other states covered by grid operator PJM — where data centers have skyrocketed demand, pushing some costs onto residential customers. But multiple studies by different researchers and organizations have failed to find a strong connection between data centers and the overall trajectory of U.S. electricity prices in recent years. Another analysis earlier this year by researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology found that, between 2010 and 2024, data centers increased average electricity prices for residential customers by just 2.1 percent. Last year, research from the Brattle Group and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found that data centers were actually decreasing costs in certain regions. And another study by the Electric Power Research Institute found that a doubling of data center capacity between 2019 and 2024 resulted in a 4 percent drop in home electricity prices. Most Read From The Washington Post Colom’s lead grows over Hyde-Smith in Mississippi race amid legal saber-rattling Hegseth not under consideration to be appointed to Senate Judge halts Trump’s arch after federal panel approves it Sullivan and Peltola remain neck-and-neck in Alaska Senate race Two more DOJ officials resign, including head of national security division “Depending on which techniques you use, you can identify a slight increase or decrease in prices historically” due to data centers, said Ryan Hledik, principal at the Brattle Group. “None of these are the kind of earth-shattering rate impacts you hear about.” The new Harvard and Penn study found a slightly higher impact on industrial electricity prices — the price paid by manufacturers and large facilities. For those customers, data centers were responsible for 15 percent of the price increase between 2020 and 2025. But for ordinary Americans, Netessine said, the changes simply were not substantial. “So far we have no evidence that data centers increase prices all that much,” Netessine said. Instead, he said, prices are rising due to more quotidian factors: rising gas prices, an aging electricity grid, and wildfires and hurricanes requiring improvements to the grid and recovery after disaster. Most of the cost of generating and delivering electricity is based on large, up-front capital costs, such as the costs to build power plants, wires and transmission lines to carry that power into homes. Some areas of the United States also have excess “capacity” in the grid — meaning that the grid is overbuilt for the actual demand. In those areas, adding a data center means that large fixed grid costs are spread over more consumers. That could lower prices. Of course, that’s not the case everywhere. PJM has had booming data center growth that has also required additional build-out of the power grid. This has raised prices at power capacity auctions, and states like Maryland have seen increasing residential prices that are at least in part from this boom. If the number of data centers continue to boom, experts say, residential prices could be affected more down the line. Data center electricity demand is expected to increase steeply over the next few years, requiring new power generation — wind, solar or natural gas — to be put onto the grid. And residents have issues with data centers that go beyond the price of electricity. The new developments have been singled out for loud noise , polluting power generation , and for disturbing residential neighborhoods and natural landscapes. According to the Pew Research Center, more than half of Americans say that data centers are mostly bad for the environment. Others feel that the AI race — which could ultimately leave many Americans out of work — is being forced upon them. “I think generally what we’re seeing is a broader range of reasons the public has opposed data centers,” Hledik said. “Concern about AI leading to loss of jobs — all of that is getting packaged together.” This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://www.washingtonpost.com/climate-environment/2026/11/06/data-centers-may-not-be-raising-americans-electricity-bills-that-much/

articles.title: 三方下周重启谈判，立场分歧依然巨大，美总统称将就俄乌达成“重大协议”，乌方称“不指望取得突破”
articles.summary: 美俄乌三方将于下周在阿联酋阿布扎比重启谈判，这是三方时隔9个月再次举行面对面会谈 。尽管美国总统特朗普高调宣称将达成涵盖整个欧洲的"庞大而美妙的协议"，但乌克兰官员明确表示对此次会谈不抱突破性期望，俄乌双方在领土与安全保障等核心议题上的分歧也依然悬而未决。 据环球时报援引法新社报道， 特朗普5日在白宫称，协议将不仅涵盖乌克兰，甚至可能涵盖整个欧洲，距离解决该问题已经"非常接近"。 与此同时据新华社， 乌克兰总统办公室主任布达诺夫 接受美国哥伦比亚广播公司采访时则表示， 不指望此次会谈取得突破，但承认双方同意重启面对面会谈本身也是一种进展。 在会谈即将召开之际，俄乌战场互攻力度未见减弱，欧洲援乌动作持续推进，各方围绕欧洲安全架构的谈判框架也在加速成形 。多重信号交织之下，此次阿布扎比会谈的实质成果仍充满不确定性。 特朗普放话"重大协议"，乌官员预期审慎 据法新社5日报道，特朗普当天在白宫表示： 这将是一份庞大而美妙的协议，每个人都会感到非常振奋。 美国《纽约时报》报道称， 特朗普的言论似乎指向美国试图将更广泛的欧洲安全问题纳入和平谈判框架 ，此举旨在回应俄总统普京此前提出的涉及俄与北约关系的部分要求。 美国总统特使威特科夫2日在社交媒体发文称，美方将于10日至11日在阿布扎比斡旋乌俄双方工作层级谈判， 会谈将重点讨论战后安全安排、局势降级、人道主义行动以及实现和平的后续步骤。 相较于特朗普的乐观表态，乌克兰官员的立场明显趋于保守。 布达诺夫表示，此次谈判并非最终谈判，也不是决定性谈判，双方将讨论如何为结束当前战事做好准备。乌克兰外长瑟比加则强调，没有乌克兰参与，就不能就乌克兰问题作出任何决定；没有欧洲参与，也不能就欧洲安全问题作出任何决定。 乌方列出优先议题，俄乌核心分歧未弥合 乌克兰外长瑟比加6日在波兰华沙举行的记者会上明确列出乌方在阿布扎比会谈中的优先议题，包括： 安全保障、黑海局势降级、能源停火、遣返乌克兰儿童以及交换战俘 。他表示，乌方非常认真地对待此次会谈，希望俄方同样认真对待。 然而，俄乌之间的核心矛盾短期内难以化解。据俄"news.ru"新闻网等媒体5日报道， 俄乌双方在领土、安全保障等核心问题上立场差异依然巨大，冲突或难以在短期内完全得到政治解决。 articles.title: 华尔街预计美国债务上限将于2月触顶，"X日期"或在2027年底前到来
articles.summary: 美国债务上限问题再度逼近。华尔街主要金融机构预计，美国财政部最早将于今年2月触及41.1万亿美元的法定借债上限，届时将不得不动用非常规会计手段维持政府运转，而真正的资金耗尽时刻——即所谓"X日期"——预计落在2027年8月至11月之间。 11月6日，据彭博报道，美国银行、巴克莱和摩根士丹利的策略师均指出，美国财政部最新融资估算显示， 今年1月至3月净借款规模约为8000亿美元，叠加当前较高的现金余额水平，将使触碰债务上限的时间大幅提前至2月中下旬。美国银行此前的预测为5月前后触顶。 目前美国政府债务距41.1万亿美元上限尚不足8000亿美元。美国财政部上周公布的数据还显示，其目标是将3月末现金余额维持在1万亿美元，创下季末目标历史纪录。 这一高现金储备安排，意味着剩余借款空间将以更快速度消耗。在国会就是否上调或暂停债务上限达成协议之前，财政部可通过非常规措施争取约3000亿至3500亿美元的额外空间，以暂时规避违约风险。 现金余额攀升加速上限触碰 美国财政部将季末现金余额目标定于1万亿美元的背后，折射出其融资策略的结构性变化。 策略师指出，美国财政部近期加大了对短期国库券的依赖，以满足政府支出和赤字融资需求。 由于短期国库券到期频率高、现金流出规模大，官员倾向于持有更大的流动性缓冲，而这反过来又以更快的速度消耗剩余的法定借款空间，从而将触顶时间大幅前移。 在国会未就债务上限采取行动的基准假设下，各机构对"X日期"的具体时点判断如下： 美国银行 预计"X日期"为2027年11月，但同时警告最早在2027年8月财政部便可能面临"令人不安的紧迫局面"； 巴克莱 基准预测为2027年8月下旬至9月初，并特别指出9月纳税季至关重要——若税收入账充裕，财政部现金跑道或可延伸至10月，使时间节点的不确定性"尤为突出"； 摩根士丹利 则预计财政部将在2027年第三季度末耗尽非常规手段，并将附息国债拍卖规模上调的节点推迟至当年11月； SMBC Nikko Securities America 认为，由于4月和5月借款能力将有所回升，财政部可能推迟至6月才启用非常规措施，并于9月或10月耗尽现金。 政治僵局风险不容忽视 债务上限谈判的政治背景同样值得关注。 民主党赢得国会多数席位，增加了其与特朗普就政府借债问题陷入长期对峙的可能性。 惠誉评级上月警告称，这一格局将加大双方"边缘博弈"的概率，除非即将卸任的共和党主导的国会能够在本届任期届满前完成上调或暂停债务上限的立法程序。 对于投资者而言，债务上限谈判的走向将直接影响短期国库券的供给节奏、货币市场流动性以及美元资产的信用预期，其市场影响不容低估。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 日央行行长：通胀存在上行风险，若未来遭遇严重冲击，或再次启用非常规宽松工具
articles.summary: 日本央行行长植田和男表示，日本通胀面临一定上行风险。随着能源相关产品价格上涨逐步传导至消费者物价，预计未来数月通胀压力可能进一步显现。 当地时间11月6日，植田在国际货币基金组织（IMF）于华盛顿举办的一场研讨会上表示， 日本央行预计基础通胀将维持在2%的目标附近，但也意识到通胀存在一些上行风险。 植田指出， 能源相关产品价格上涨已经开始影响消费者通胀，预计物价涨幅到明年年初可能进一步加快。 与此同时，日本工资增长已经与2%的通胀水平逐渐形成匹配关系。 他还表示，日本央行正在密切关注其他主要央行的政策行动，并未排除未来再次使用非常规货币政策工具的可能性。不过，如果重新部署相关工具，央行需要尽可能降低其对市场正常运行的负面影响。 能源价格传导至消费者物价，基础通胀目标仍待巩固 植田此次讲话释放出两个重要信号：能源价格上涨可能推动日本短期通胀进一步加速，而工资增长与物价之间正在形成更加符合央行目标的关系。 植田表示，能源相关产品价格上涨已经开始传导至消费者物价，预计这一影响将在明年年初进一步显现。 在工资与物价关系方面，植田表示，日本目前正处于工资增长与2%通胀相匹配的均衡状态。 不过，他同时指出，日本社会尚未普遍形成对2%通胀目标的稳定认知。日本央行当前的政策重点，是将基础通胀稳定在目标水平附近，而不仅仅是推动其达到2%。 植田为非常规宽松工具留出空间，强调控制市场副作用 对于日本央行过去使用的非常规货币政策工具，植田表示，这些措施曾产生一些积极效果，但并不能完全替代在正利率环境下降息所发挥的作用。 他指出，如果日本未来遭遇经济冲击，冲击的严重程度可能决定央行是否需要再次启用这些工具。 植田表示， 如果确实需要重新部署非常规政策工具，重要的是尽可能将通胀或基础通胀维持在2%左右，同时考虑如何减少政策带来的负面影响，包括对市场正常运行的影响。 这一表态意味着，日本央行并未完全排除未来重新使用非常规货币政策工具的可能性。 此外，植田表示， 日本央行正在非常密切地关注其他主要央行的政策行动。 这些行动会影响汇率、利率等资产价格，并通过金融市场传导至日本经济。 他强调，其他央行的政策选择也反映了其对本国经济状况的判断，因此具有重要参考价值。 植田谈AI经济影响：劳动力短缺或使日本受益于技术替代 植田还谈及人工智能对日本经济的影响。他表示， AI技术快速进步为日本经济带来了积极的需求冲击，但其对供给侧的影响仍需要进一步研究。 与一些其他国家不同，日本长期面临劳动力短缺，因此AI替代部分劳动岗位可能有利于日本经济。 IMF总裁Kristalina Georgieva则指出，近期AI相关股票走弱，反映出市场对AI投资热潮依赖程度及高估值的担忧，这些因素正在影响全球市场。 她表示，全球央行在评估抗击通胀的政策措施时，也需要考虑AI驱动的经济增长是否可能放缓。市场波动可能持续，这将增加央行维护物价稳定的难度。 植田还表达了对网络安全风险的担忧，认为网络安全问题可能影响金融稳定，部分小型银行和小企业在相关防护方面仍做得不够。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。
